claims.text: A new predictive approach can separately calculate lattice thermal conductivity in fully disordered HfNbTaTiZr without conflating it with electronic thermal conductivity.
DFT-based disordered lattice dynamics and perturbative force-constant fluctuation models can accurately represent phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
The applicable initial material is defect-free, single-phase bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen controlled near or below 1 wt.%.
The framework explicitly models mass and force-constant fluctuations to calculate phonon dispersion and scattering rates.
The approach is intended to apply from approximately 50 K to 1200 K in high-purity, near-ideal bulk samples.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Chemical disorder in HfNbTaTiZr produces local variations in atomic mass and bond stiffness.
Local mass and bond-stiffness variations alter phonon dispersion and phonon scattering.
Electronic transport remains largely independent of the disorder-induced changes affecting phonons.
DFT-derived force constants and perturbative scattering calculations capture atomic-scale disorder better than averaged analytical models.
Predicted lattice thermal conductivity will agree with an experimentally isolated lattice component to within ±20%.
The model will capture the temperature dependence below 200 K more accurately than earlier approaches.
From 300 K to 1200 K, the isolated lattice contribution will be around 10 W/(K m), near the lower end of the reported total-conductivity range.
Previous approaches have error margins exceeding 20%.
Previous approaches either conflate lattice and electronic transport or rely on simplified Debye approximations that fail to capture atomic-scale disorder.
Significant oxygen contamination or unmodeled microstructural defects may cause prediction errors larger than ±20%.
The expected improvement is roughly a 20% reduction in error relative to current analytical models.
Electrical conductivity combined with the Wiedemann-Franz relation can be used to estimate and subtract the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
Deviation of the isolated lattice thermal conductivity by more than ±20% from predictions across the measured range would falsify the hypothesis.
